questions.text: What makes a sound-classification task multi-label rather than mutually exclusive multiclass?

options.A: Every recording must contain exactly one positive class.
options.B: Every class must have the same number of training examples.
options.C: Each recording must be converted into a text transcript first.
options.D: One recording can have several positive sound labels at once.

questions.explanation: Multi-label classification allows simultaneous positive labels, such as both speech and music in one clip.

questions.text: A sound-tagging model must detect overlapping events. Which evaluation directly assesses ranking quality across its multiple labels?

options.A: Mean average precision across sound classes.
options.B: Only top-1 accuracy after forcing one label per clip.
options.C: Only the number of audio frames per recording.
options.D: Word error rate on an unrelated speech transcript.

questions.explanation: mAP evaluates class-wise label rankings and is appropriate for multi-label audio tagging; forcing one label would discard overlapping events.

questions.text: The k-NN code selects the three highest cosine similarities, then returns the majority label. Neighbors in descending similarity are [(0.95, "dog"), (0.90, "siren"), (0.85, "siren"), (0.20, "dog")]. What does k=3 return?

options.A: "dog", because the closest neighbor always decides.
options.B: "siren", because it has two of the three selected votes.
options.C: Both labels, because k-NN always returns all labels.
options.D: An error, because similarities must sum to one.

questions.explanation: The top three labels are dog, siren, siren. The supplied classifier uses majority voting, so siren wins.
